15 of the 33 major central banks, or 45%, have raised interest rates over the last 6 months, the largest proportion since 2023.

By comparison, the proportion peaked at ~95% in 2022, following post-pandemic stimulus and the resulting surge in global inflation.

In total, 54 central banks have hiked rates so far in 2026.

This also marks the first time since September 2023 that more central banks have hiked than cut rates over a rolling 3-month period.

"Higher for longer" is back.

a16z's Martin Casado with https://t.co/URbd8O8R0Z CTO Owen He on why a lot of RSI pitches are selling something as old as the steam engine:

Martin: "I see a lot of pitches come in, and a lot of them use the term RSI. And I'll be like, 'Oh, so what do you do?' And they'll say, 'We use AI to create AI.' 'That sounds very interesting. So what do you do?' 'We use AI to create GPU kernels.'"

Owen: "RSI is definitely an overloaded term today... The important thing when you are differentiating them is to ask the question, what is the optimizer and what is the optimizee? When you're self-improving, who is improving?"

"There are people who are saying, 'Okay, we're doing RSI. We have humans using AI to develop better AI.' But that to us is just autocatalysis... the ideas and the improvement come from human brains."

Martin: "Most technical epochs have had autocatalytic effects. There's no way you can create a computer chip without a computer... You could build better steam engines because you could get coal faster, etc. So this notion of using the thing to build the thing faster is not new."

Owen: "That human brain was never the optimizee. Now, for the first time, we could swap the optimizer as the optimizee... The brain of the agents, which is the LLM, the model, can be the thing that you're optimizing, and this leads to this reinvestment of cognitive improvement into itself."

A lot of RSI pitches are really just people using AI to build better AI. Tech has always worked that way. You needed computers to build chips. Steam engines got better once you could get coal faster.

Dhaval and Owen's bar is higher. The model has to improve itself: its weights, its harness, even the prompt that tells it what to work on next.

And the gains have to hold up when you count what they cost. They track everyone's experiment spend on a "bleeder board," and one engineer, the Viceroy of Variance, has the job of breaking their results.

Over the past few months, they've started seeing early signs of their system getting better and cheaper at the same time.

BREAKING: Global physical gold-backed ETFs attracted +$30.7 billion in inflows in Q3 2026, their largest quarterly intake on record.

In September, inflows totaled +$10 billion, the 3rd-largest monthly inflow of 2026, following +$17.9 billion in August, the 2nd-largest monthly intake on record.

As a result, global gold ETF holdings rose +67 tonnes last month to a record 4,256 tonnes.

This surpasses the previous record of 4,176 tonnes set in February.

Year-to-date, global gold ETFs have seen +$38.5 billion in inflows, equivalent to an increase of +226 tonnes in gold holdings, with all regions recording positive demand.

UK-listed funds have attracted +$9.5 billion in inflows over the same period, overtaking China to become the largest source of country-level demand so far in 2026.

Demand for gold is extremely strong.

Since mid-September, 12-month hike pricing has shrunk across almost every major economy. Australia down 47 basis points, the euro zone down 43, Korea down 22, the US down 19. Only China nudged higher.

Fewer hikes ahead takes pressure off long yields, and that is a tailwind for risk assets.

Right now I'm rebuilding my entire macro database from scratch. Anyone who knows how many charts I typically work with knows that's a fairly daunting task.

The unexpected benefit is that it forces me to revisit everything I've ever built with a fresh pair of eyes. Charts, indicators, and business cycle frameworks I've used for years are being questioned, rebuilt, and improved.

The charts are coming back, and they'll be better than ever. Expect all the usual macro chart mayhem to return next month…
